title: Trophic support delays but does not prevent cell‐intrinsic degeneration of neurons deficient for munc18‐1
abstract: The stability of neuronal networks is thought to depend on synaptic transmission which provides activity-dependent maintenance signals for both synapses and neurons. Here, we tested the relationship between presynaptic secretion and neuronal maintenance using munc18-1-null mutant mice as a model. These mutants have a specific defect in secretion from synaptic and large dense-cored vesicles [Verhage et al. (2000), Science, 287, 864-869; Voets et al. (2001), Neuron, 31, 581-591]. Neuronal networks in these mutants develop normally up to synapse formation but eventually degenerate. The proposed relationship between secretion and neuronal maintenance was tested in low-density and organotypic cultures and, in vivo, by conditional cell-specific inactivation of the munc18-1 gene. Dissociated munc18-1-deficient neurons died within 4 days in vitro (DIV). Application of trophic factors, insulin or BDNF delayed degeneration up to 7 DIV. In organotypic cultures, munc18-1-deficient neurons survived until 9 DIV. On glial feeders, these neurons survived up to 10 DIV and 14 DIV when insulin was applied. Co-culturing dissociated mutant neurons with wild-type neurons did not prolong survival beyond 4 DIV, but coculturing mutant slices with wild-type slices prolonged survival up to 19 DIV. Cell-specific deletion of munc18-1 expression in cerebellar Purkinje cells in vivo resulted in the specific loss of these neurons without affecting connected or surrounding neurons. Together, these data allow three conclusions. First, the lack of synaptic activity cannot explain the degeneration in munc18-1-null mutants. Second, trophic support delays but cannot prevent degeneration. Third, a cell-intrinsic yet unknown function of munc18-1 is essential for prolonged survival.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2004 neuroscience article has sustained scholarly uptake, with 68 citations in OpenAlex and 69 documented downstream reuse events. Its influence is concentrated in research on synaptic transmission, vesicle trafficking, and STXBP1/Munc18-1 biology, including recent citations in high-visibility journals and preprints. The citation record suggests continuing relevance rather than a short-lived burst of attention.

Full narrative

The article argues that trophic support can delay, but not stop, cell-intrinsic degeneration in neurons lacking munc18-1, using mutant mice to probe how presynaptic secretion relates to neuronal maintenance. That core idea has proven durable: the work has 68 citations in OpenAlex, a percentile value of 0.63226217, and 69 downstream reuse events across articles, preprints, a review, a dissertation, a book chapter, and other scholarly outputs. The citation pattern indicates steady, field-level use over time rather than a single peak.

The strongest impact signal is scholarly reuse in mechanistic neuroscience. The citing landscape is led by journals such as the Journal of Neuroscience, Brain, eLife, Journal of Neurochemistry, Journal of Biological Chemistry, PLoS ONE, and Neuron, with the dominant concepts centered on cellular transport and secretion, neuroscience, and neuropharmacology. Recent citing works continue to revisit STXBP1/Munc18-1 in epilepsy, synaptic function, and vesicle replenishment, showing that the article remains relevant to active questions about presynaptic machinery and neurodevelopmental disease.

Scite also shows engagement with the paper’s claims: 2 supporting citation statements and 1 contradicting statement. That mix suggests the work is still being discussed as part of an evolving evidence base, with some direct support and some critical or alternative interpretation in the literature. The public-discourse record is sparse here, so the impact story is primarily scholarly rather than media-facing.

The article is available through a green open-access route, with an open repository instance recorded in the Netherlands. Its authorship spans multiple neuroscience-centered institutions, and the reuse profile is international, with the United States and the Netherlands especially prominent among citing works. Overall, the record shows a paper that has become a durable reference point for studies of synaptic secretion, neuronal maintenance, and STXBP1-linked disease mechanisms.
